name: Converse XMPP agent-coordination daemon
description: This project uses XMPP as a coordination layer for multiple LLM coding agents. A Converse XMPP client runs as a headless NodeJS daemon with a CLI that agents can invoke, and a /coordination skill (enabled by default via a Claude Code hook) ensures the daemon is running and has each agent join a password-restricted, members-only MUC shared with the other agents in the workspace and the human. Agents announce their tasks and statuses in the groupchat, coordinate so that when one agent's PR is merged the others become aware, rebase their own PRs and fix conflicts, and hand off newly arising sidequests to parallel Herdr tabs by asking in the MUC whether other agents are idle. Tasks can be assigned via XMPP DMs, groupchat, or Claude Code. Planned extensions include using PubSub to power a web UI with vertical swimlanes showing which agents are active, what they are working on, and for how long. The tools are harness-neutral and not locked to any particular inference provider.

description: An abstract distributed systems programming language that offers fine-grained control over resources while requiring developers to express their intent to the compiler rather than declaring machinery directly. name: Orpheum
description: A self-hosted media server for video, comparable to Plex or Jellyfin, shipping as a single Go binary deployed via Docker with a beta opening in about a month. It reaches a home server from anywhere with no port forwarding, VPN, or paywall (even behind carrier-grade NAT), supports casting to any logged-in device, and watch-together playback with synced video and voice chat that can be mixed with casting. Playback features include dialogue boost and loudness levelling per film, adaptive quality tuned for a home's upload bandwidth, and hardware transcoding with full quality in supported browsers. The library scanner explains its matches and flags guesses, and shows missing disks instead of silently vanishing titles. Data ownership is emphasized: the database is a rebuildable index, metadata corrections write back as NFO files readable by Kodi and Jellyfin, and automatic backups preserve non-derivable data (watch state, preferences, shares). Security is a primary concern: the network-facing core never opens media files or runs FFmpeg; a separate network-isolated media node handles file reads and transcodes over Unix sockets; FFmpeg is sandboxed with Landlock and seccomp; there is a small allowlisted dependency tree with pure Go and no cgo, secrets sealed at rest, optional read-only library mounting so a compromise cannot encrypt or delete media, and a cryptographically signed chain for servers and releases.
problem: Existing media servers impose paywalls, bandwidth limiting, crippled behavior, and required logins, and remote access usually demands port forwarding, a VPN, or tools like Tailscale; meanwhile the increasing pace of hacks, CVEs, and AI-assisted intrusion makes security a primary concern.

name: Bonsai
description: A voxel game engine under development for ~10 years. The world and objects in it are represented as SDF (density) fields, and the world generator and editor operate almost entirely on the GPU via a fused three-stage 'ubershader' pipeline: a user-configurable GLSL 'shaping' shader, a fused stage that convolves normals, runs a user-configurable 'decoration' function, and interprets SDF edits compiled from a graph into bytecode, and a final stage that packs occupancy, color, and normal into 32 bits. GPU results are passed back to the CPU for entity/structure spawning callbacks, then chunks are meshed with a fast binary algorithm and uploaded, retaining 16 bits per surface voxel and scaling to world sizes greater than 1B voxels cubed. The engine aims to give users both easy-to-use tools and granular control over the final output, while remaining fast.
